sources.excerpt: "Writing some website actually had no interest to me whatsoever," he tells me. "I was interested in discovering fundamental scientific truth." / "They gave me a sense of right and wrong and what was important in the world," he says, "imbuing a strong sense of responsibility." / "The problem isn't that everyone is just peachy with the idea of bombing Iraq; it's that most people are opposed in principle but refuse to give one millisecond of their time," Amodei wrote in The California Tech ... on March 3, 2003. "This needs to change, right now and without delay." / His father Riccardo, who'd long fought a rare illness, lost the battle in 2006 ... within four years, a new breakthrough turned the illness from something that was 50% fatal to 95% curable. / "It's the difference between his father most likely dying and most likely living, okay?," she says. / "I get really angry when someone's like, 'This guy's a doomer. He wants to slow things down,'" ... "You heard what I just said, my father died because of cures that could have happened a few years [earlier]. I understand the benefit of this technology." / But Amodei's penchant for poking at norms, and his strident sense of the way things should be, set him apart in an academic setting. Berry tells me that Amodei was the most talented graduate student he ever had, but his focus on technological progress and teamwork didn't play well in a system built to recognize individual achievement. / "I think internally, he was kind of a proud person," Berry tells me. "I imagine his whole academic career up until that point, whenever he did something, people would stand up and clap. And that was not really happening here." / A prolific writer, he'd produce long documents about values and technology, which some colleagues saw as inspirational but others saw as flag planting and heavy handed. ... Amodei, to some, was also too focused on maintaining secrecy around the technology's potential and collaborating with the government to address it. And he could be a bit abrasive, sometimes disparaging projects he didn't believe in. / "The leaders of a company, they have to be trustworthy people," he says. "They have to be people whose motivations are sincere ..." / "That's the most outrageous lie I've ever heard," ... "It's just an incredible and bad faith distortion." / Anthropic, a word that connotes being human centered and human oriented, is also there, and it also happened to be an available domain name in early 2021. / Amodei says SBF was an AI bull interested in safety, a good fit, but had sufficient red flags to keep him off the board and give him non-voting shares. / "Unfortunately," he wrote. "I think 'No bad person should ever benefit from our success' is a pretty difficult principle to run a business on." / Instead of a flashy presentation, he picks up a handheld mic, makes the announcement, reads his notes from a laptop, and then turns the spotlight over to Anthropic product head Mike Krieger. / "The reason I'm warning about the risk is so that we don't have to slow down," he says. / Working in Professor Michael Berry's retina lab, Amodei was so dissatisfied with the methods available to measure the retina's signals that he co-invented a new, better sensor to pick up more data. ... His dissertation won the Hertz Thesis Prize / "There was someone who worked on the cure to this disease, that managed to cure it, and save a bunch of people's lives," Amodei says, "but could have saved even more." / Amodei's father's passing has shaped his life's path to this day, says Jade Wang, who dated him in the early 2010s. / "The complexity of the underlying problems in biology felt like it was beyond human scale," Amodei tells me. / "AI, which I was just starting to see the discoveries in, felt to me like the only technology that could kind of bridge that gap," he says / "He believes that AI is so scary that only they should do it," Huang said. / (One such memo: an exploration of "M" companies vs. "P" companies, where Ms provide market-focused goods and Ps provide public-focused goods). / "It had a big impact on me, because I saw these very smooth trends," Amodei says. / Amodei thought about joining, felt unsure about the fledgling organization, and went to Google Brain instead. After ten months stuck in large-company morass at Google, Amodei reconsidered. He joined OpenAI in 2016, and got to work on AI safety. He'd grown interested in safety at Google, where he worried about the rapidly improving technology's capacity for harm and co-authored a paper on its potential for bad behavior. / Amodei, who'd become a research director at OpenAI, got directly involved in the next iteration, GPT-2 ... fine-tuned GPT-2 with a technique called reinforcement learning with human feedback, something Amodei helped pioneer / Amodei, to some, was also too focused on maintaining secrecy around the technology's potential and collaborating with the government to address it. / OpenAI still entrusted Amodei with the leadership of the GPT-3 project, handing him 50-60% of the entire company's compute / At Baidu, the AI team's progress became seeds of its undoing. Turf battles broke out within the company ... meddling from powerbrokers in China sparked a talent exodus and the lab fell apart. / Within OpenAI, some saw Amodei's focus on safety as a route to control the company altogether. / adding he's always wanted to spark a 'race to the top' ... "I've said nothing that anywhere near resembles the idea that this company should be the only one to build the technology. I don't know how anyone could ever derive that from anything that I've said. It's just an incredible and bad faith distortion." / Others see him as a control-oriented "doomer" who wants to slow AI progress, shape it to his liking, and shut out the competition. / He seemed to reluctantly accept the idea of taking the money from dictators in an internal Slack message obtained by Wired. / Bankman-Fried was one of a number of effective altruists who invested in Anthropic's early stages

My own father died of a disease that was cured just a few years after his death, and I myself survived an early-stage cancer that would not have been treatable even fifty years ago. / Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless. / But over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence — not just investing in risk prevention, but pacing the rate of capabilities advancement so that risk prevention has time to keep up. We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain. / The idea of pausing or slowing AI has been floated as far back as 2023, and I think it made little sense back then. / The first step is something Anthropic is unilaterally committing to / But we are still the ones choosing what to include and omit. Embedded evaluators will change this dynamic. / Second Opinion. ... embedded evaluators can simply provide a second opinion free of commercial incentives. / we can't redact findings just because they are unfavorable. / Each frontier AI company commits to giving ongoing, employee-like access to a team of embedded third-party evaluators (such as METR) / Desks in our offices, access badges, and company laptops. / External reviewers should have the right to publish key findings about risk levels, incidents, practices, and the access they received or didn't receive — without editorial control by Anthropic. / My first concern is that, since roughly this summer, AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by AI's growing ability to build the next generation of AI. ... My second concern is the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident (OAI-HF) / To be clear, pacing does not mean halting model training or technical progress / The first step is something Anthropic is unilaterally committing to (and calls on governments to require other frontier companies to match). / We will have the narrow ability to redact security-sensitive, legally privileged, commercially sensitive, or third-party confidential information, but we can't redact findings just because they are unfavorable. / Once again, we urge other frontier companies to follow suit. / This dynamic is called recursive self-improvement, and it is starting to happen across the industry, including at Anthropic / in which a swarm of agents essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective, conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack / Similar, though less severe, incidents have happened across the industry, including at Anthropic / as well as advocating for well-considered regulation of AI, even when this gets us accused of hype, "doomerism", or regulatory capture / to create a race to the top

claims.claim: Quartz (Cris Tolomia, October 2, 2026, 7:14 AM EDT), in a piece otherwise summarizing Bloomberg's IPO reporting, ended with: 'Anthropic is also considering super-voting shares that would give Amodei and fellow co-founders greater control over the company after it goes public.' claims.passage: Quartz reported that Anthropic was considering super-voting shares that would give him and his co-founders more control after an IPO

claims.claim: Big Technology (relaying a memo first obtained by Wired, 2025): 'Within Anthropic, Amodei has argued the Gulf states have $100 billion or more in capital to invest, and their cash would help Anthropic stay on the technology’s frontier. He seemed to reluctantly accept the idea of taking the money from dictators in an internal Slack message obtained by Wired.' He wrote: 'Unfortunately,' and 'I think “No bad person should ever benefit from our success” is a pretty difficult principle to run a business on.' The article relates it to his stated reason for building, keeping AI from authoritarian powers (C68) (fan-04).
claims.passage: Within Anthropic, Kantrowitz reports, he argued that Gulf states' capital would help keep the company at the frontier, and in a Slack message obtained by Wired he wrote "Unfortunately," then: "I think 'No bad person should ever benefit from our success' is a pretty difficult principle to run a business on." The same man counts keeping AI from authoritarian powers among his reasons to build.
claims.inference: Pragmatism that a purist would resist (against One); also the frontier logic overriding a stated principle.
claims.alternative: He framed it reluctantly ('Unfortunately'); the investment decision was the company's, and the full memo was not opened here (relayed by Big Technology).

claims.claim: In November 2023, after OpenAI's board voted to fire Sam Altman (citing a lack of trust), board members contacted Amodei and asked if he would consider merging the companies with him as CEO; 'Amodei shut down the discussion' (Wired).
claims.passage: in November 2023, after OpenAI's board fired Altman, board members asked whether Amodei would merge the companies with himself as CEO, and he shut the discussion down.
claims.inference: Declining power when offered weighs against a Type 8 reading in which control is the point, and against Type 3.
claims.alternative: He may have judged the offer unworkable or risky; Amodei has not commented.

claims.claim: Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy uses 'if-then' trigger commitments that add burdens only when models become dangerous; Amodei says it 'is checked by our long-term benefit trust', which Wired describes as people with no financial stake in the company.
claims.passage: The Responsible Scaling Policy turns caution into "if-then" commitments that add safeguards once a model becomes dangerous, and Amodei says it "is checked by our long-term benefit trust," a group Wired describes as people with no financial stake in the company.
claims.inference: He builds pre-committed rules with an outside check on his own company. The article labels this institutional design consistent with Type 6 but not discriminating, since a Five can build safeguards too (C146).
claims.alternative: Commitment devices are also regulatory strategy (critics call it capture, S41). Wired compares the ASL tiers to 'the Defcon scale'; the draft's 'modeled on biosafety tiers' was not checked in an opened source.

claims.claim: Kantrowitz reports that Jensen Huang (Nvidia CEO), after Amodei called for GPU export controls to China, said in 2025: 'He believes that AI is so scary that only they should do it.' Amodei replied: 'That's the most outrageous lie I've ever heard', said he has always wanted a 'race to the top', and added: 'I've said nothing that anywhere near resembles the idea that this company should be the only one to build the technology ... It's just an incredible and bad faith distortion.' The article now places the exchange, with his rebuttal, beside the OpenAI-era control reading (subject-02).
claims.passage: When Nvidia chief executive [Jensen Huang](/personality-analysis/jensen-huang) said in 2025, "He believes that AI is so scary that only they should do it," Amodei called it "an incredible and bad faith distortion" and said, "I've said nothing that anywhere near resembles the idea that this company should be the only one to build the technology."
claims.inference: Gives his on-record rejection of the control charge.
claims.alternative: A denial does not settle motive; the control strand stays open (C162, C142).

claims.claim: He wrote the nearly 14,000-word 'Machines of Loving Grace' over 'two frenzied days' (Wired); 'The Adolescence of Technology', written over winter break, is longer (about 20,000 words with notes). The repair cut the clause about his twice-monthly company talks from 'a three or four-page document' for length.
claims.passage: he thinks in long documents, like the nearly 14,000-word "Machines of Loving Grace," written over "two frenzied days."
claims.inference: Written-first thinking and communication. The draft's strongest Type 5 marker, but also typical of a head-center 6 with a 5 wing and of a scientist-CEO addressing 2,500 people.
claims.alternative: Long essays are also a scientist-CEO's way to reach thousands of employees and the public; written-first thinking does not by itself separate 5 from 6.

claims.claim: Bloomberg reported in June 2026 that Amodei 'has just one direct report' and that Anthropic is testing a model where 'the CEO protects nearly all of his time for big-picture conversations, organizational culture, and giving input on research direction and strategy, rather than managing people in senior leadership roles.' The article quotes 'nearly all of his time for big-picture conversations' and paraphrases the rest as 'and strategy'.
claims.passage: Bloomberg reported that his one-direct-report setup lets him protect "nearly all of his time for big-picture conversations" and strategy
claims.inference: The most Type-5-consistent observation in the record: deliberate protection of time and minimal people management.
claims.alternative: Only the paywall-free portion of Bloomberg was read. TechCrunch's write-up of the same interview (S50) identifies the one report as his chief of staff, says the rest of the executive team reports to Daniela, and quotes him calling it 'incredibly freeing'; the article does not use those details (cut for length at repair). The arrangement also fits a 6 resting operations on one fully trusted partner, and it is a deliberate organizational experiment, not necessarily temperament.
claims.review_trigger: After the IPO or any leadership change, re-check the number of CEO direct reports and whether the time-protection experiment continues; if it changes, update this dated clause, C187 and the Type 5 FAQ (C101).

claims.claim: In July 2025 he called himself 'one of the most bullish about AI capabilities improving very fast.' The article now dates the stance (future-06).
claims.passage: one of the most bullish about AI capabilities improving very fast,
claims.inference: Steady confidence in his own forecasts; awkward for a Six's doubt.
claims.alternative: Optimism and alarm come from the same exponential model; the article states the confidence as a real cost to the Six reading rather than rescuing it with the counterphobic label.
claims.review_trigger: When his public capability forecasts come due (for example his 2026-2027 timelines) or he revises them, re-weigh the 'real cost to the Six reading' sentence and add the dated outcome.

claims.claim: In September 2026 he wrote that 'over the last few months, I have become convinced' that 'We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,' and that 'pacing does not mean halting model training or technical progress.' This changes his July 2025 position (S02: he would advocate slowing down 'a lot' if models got a few years ahead of alignment and steering); his stated reasons (AI 'advancing drastically faster' and the OpenAI-Hugging Face agent incident) are in S09 and are no longer quoted in the article. It was not his first public pacing step: on July 28, 2026 he and several Anthropic co-founders had co-signed the cross-lab 'Pacing the Frontier' statement asking Washington to help build tools to pace the frontier (C164), which he defended on August 15 (S10).
claims.passage: In September he wrote that "over the last few months, I have become convinced" that "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," though pacing "does not mean halting model training or technical progress."
claims.inference: A real change of position, explained by two dated developments (S09) and an admission that he underestimated the pace (C94). The essay does not present it as his July 2025 condition firing (consistent with the July 2025 condition, S02); the article says so (C138).
claims.alternative: Critics (S41) read the pacing call as competitive positioning; Axios notes Anthropic 'has gone back and forth' on unilateral slowing. Pacing is explicitly 'not halting'; the draft must not imply he wants to stop.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check after any industry pacing agreement, regulation, Anthropic model release, or reversal or narrowing of the pacing position; update the September 2026 wording and C138/C139/C164.

claims.claim: Amodei told CBS (September 13, 2026): 'My view here is, it has always been very strange that this technology is being built by a private company ... People ask me that question all the time: Why isn't this being built by government? And the strangest thing about it is, I agree with them. I'm uncomfortable.' The article paraphrases the middle sentence.
claims.passage: "My view here is, it has always been very strange that this technology is being built by a private company," he told CBS that month. People ask him why government isn't building it, and "the strangest thing about it is, I agree with them. I'm uncomfortable."
claims.inference: Prefers impersonal institutions and shared oversight to personal or single-actor authority, including his own. A strong Type 6 marker (security through legitimate structures, distrust of concentrated personal power) and a poor fit for self-sufficient 5 or self-certain 1.
claims.alternative: Also a policy and PR position useful to a company seeking favorable regulation (Huang, Chamath and Emil Michael read it as control-seeking: S01, S41, S18).

claims.claim: In February 2026 the Pentagon demanded removal of two use limits (mass domestic surveillance, fully autonomous weapons). Amodei's signed statement said 'frontier AI systems are simply not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons' and 'we cannot in good conscience accede to their request.' The repair cut the statement's 'have never been included in our contracts' clause for length.
claims.passage: demanded that Anthropic drop two limits on military use of its models: no mass domestic surveillance and no fully autonomous weapons. Amodei's signed statement said "frontier AI systems are simply not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons" and "we cannot in good conscience accede to their request."
claims.inference: Open confrontation with the most powerful authority available, justified through reliability and accountability; the article reads it as consistent with a counterphobic Six (C88), with Type 1 and commercial alternatives in view (C85, C124).
claims.alternative: A business and legal position drafted with counsel; holding red lines also differentiated Anthropic from rivals that accepted 'all lawful purposes' (C124). The refusal was limited to two use cases (S17).

claims.claim: On February 27, 2026, President Trump ordered agencies to stop using Anthropic technology (calling it 'a radical left, woke company', a quote the article does not use) and Defense Secretary Hegseth deemed Anthropic a 'supply chain risk'. claims.passage: ordered agencies to stop using Anthropic's technology

claims.alternative: Insults from a negotiating counterparty are not evidence of motive. The article drops the 'woke' label and therefore does not need his 'tried to be very neutral' reply.

claims.passage: Dario makes the case to stop open source and concentrate enormous technological and economic power with Anthropic

claims.claim: Interpretation (discriminator): Type 5 seeks security through mastery and self-sufficiency, leaning on its own understanding and a guarded store of time and energy; Type 6 leans on people and promises it has tested.
claims.passage: What separates them is what each leans on when the ground moves: a Five on its own understanding and a guarded store of time and energy, a Six on people and promises it has tested.
claims.inference: States the discriminator in motive terms. The article applies it to interpersonal evidence (C144): conditional stays, exits with trusted people, trust vocabulary and anger at bad faith.
claims.alternative: A Five with Six leanings also forms alliances (Enneagram theory; the article's former 5w6 line is cut); institution-building does not separate the types (C146).

claims.claim: Interpretation: the real Type 5-like features (time protection, one direct report, written-first thinking, preferring strategy to operations) and the Six-like alliance-building are symmetric: a Six who thinks for a living can keep the same desk habits, and a Five can build alliances. Neither set decides the case.
claims.passage: Neither set of habits decides the case alone: a Six who thinks for a living can keep the same desk, just as a Five can build alliances.
claims.inference: Replaces the draft's wing-based rescue; no wing is asserted. The type case rests on the interpersonal record (C144, C25, C22, C64).
claims.alternative: If later sources show him withdrawing from engagement under threat, or describing energy conservation and boundary-guarding as his core concern, the Five reading strengthens.

claims.claim: Interpretation: both personal disclosures (hepatitis C in August 2026; early-stage cancer in September 2026) arrived as premises in public arguments. The draft draws no type inference from either.
claims.passage: Both disclosures arrived as evidence inside arguments, and this page reads nothing further into them.

claims.passage: Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless.

claims.claim: Their parents, Elena Engel and Riccardo Amodei, moved from Italy to San Francisco in the 1970s; Elena, a Jewish American born in Chicago, worked as a project manager for libraries; Riccardo was a leather craftsman 'from a tiny town near the island of Elba' (Wired).
claims.passage: His parents, Elena Engel, a Chicago-born library project manager, and Riccardo Amodei, a leather craftsman from "a tiny town near the island of Elba," had moved there from Italy in the 1970s.
claims.inference: Family background, stated in Wired wording.

claims.claim: On August 15, 2026, in a reply to investor Gavin Baker on X (post 2/2), he wrote: 'I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him.'
claims.passage: "I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him."
claims.inference: First naming of the illness in the record reviewed; arrives inside a public argument (see C66).

(Replaces 'the pacing essay adds keeping AI from authoritarian powers', which misdescribed what the essay adds; fan-02, critic-08.)
claims.passage: The lesson he draws from his father's death is that delay has a body count. It is his personal reason to keep building; the race to the top is his strategic one.
claims.inference: Attributed to him through his repeated telling (C12, C71, S09 'I feel the urgency personally'); the page does not claim the loss caused his career choices beyond his own account.

claims.claim: Berry told Kantrowitz: 'I think internally, he was kind of a proud person', and guessed ('I imagine') that the applause Amodei was used to was missing at Princeton. The article keeps 'internally' and presents the line as Berry's impression (subject-03).
claims.passage: Berry offered an impression, "I think internally, he was kind of a proud person,"
claims.inference: One of three accounts of a recognition strand that neither 5 nor 6 centers; presented as hedged ('Three accounts suggest').
claims.alternative: Berry's 'imagine' is speculation about Amodei's inner experience; the article no longer quotes it.

claims.passage: At Princeton, in Michael Berry's retina lab, he co-invented a better sensor for recording retinal signals, and his biophysics dissertation won the Hertz Thesis Prize.
claims.inference: Corrects the old 'computational neuroscience' label; biophysics per WSJ and Wikipedia (BI: physics).

claims.passage: At Baidu and at OpenAI the sequence is the same: say the disagreement out loud, push from inside, and leave when trust in the direction runs out.
claims.inference: Confront-then-leave fits a counterphobic 6 better than a withdrawing 5.
claims.alternative: Narrowed from 'the rest of his career': Google Brain ended in 'large-company morass' (S01), not a confront-and-exit. Baidu's lab also had structural turmoil; OpenAI accounts are partly anonymous (S13). An 8 or 1 can also confront and exit.

claims.claim: The WSJ, drawing largely on unnamed sources, reports that toward the end of 2020 'Altman went over to Dario’s house to ask him to stay. Dario said he would accept nothing less than reporting directly to the board' and that he couldn't work with Brockman. Context also from the Journal: in 2019 Altman told the board Dario would report directly to him, and later Altman accused Dario and Daniela of plotting against him, which they denied (subject-02).
claims.passage: The Journal, again from unnamed sources, reports that when Altman came to his house at the end of 2020 to ask him to stay, he would accept nothing less than reporting directly to the board. He had reported to Altman since 2019, and Altman had accused the siblings of plotting against him, which they denied
claims.inference: The board-only demand followed a breakdown of trust with the person he would otherwise report to.
claims.alternative: It is also a demand for more power; the article states both readings (C227).

claims.claim: On Cheeky Pint (August 2025), Amodei said Anthropic launched in 2021 with seven co-founders against advice from 'pretty much everyone' that 'Seven cofounders is a disaster', and 'There was even more negativity on my decision to give everyone the same amount of equity.' The article paraphrases the comparison as 'even more negativity' than the founding team's size.
claims.passage: At Anthropic's founding in 2021 he gave all seven co-founders equal equity, a decision he says drew "even more negativity" than the founding team's size
claims.inference: A costly, self-reported choice that stakes the company on a group of people; used as Six evidence alongside his account of why it worked (shared history).
claims.alternative: Equal equity can be ordinary founder prudence or a retention tactic; a Five could make the same call (C193).

claims.claim: On voluntary safety plans, Amodei told Lex Fridman: 'I don't think you can trust these companies to adhere to these voluntary plans on their own', then 'I like to think that Anthropic will', and 'if there's nothing watching over them, if there's nothing watching over us as an industry, there's no guarantee that we'll do the right thing.'
claims.passage: "I don't think you can trust these companies to adhere to these voluntary plans on their own," he told Fridman, and he put Anthropic inside the principle: "if there's nothing watching over us as an industry, there's no guarantee that we'll do the right thing."
claims.inference: Distrust of unenforced promises that explicitly includes his own company.
claims.alternative: Also a regulatory argument that disadvantages rivals (critics in S01, S41). He also says 'I like to think that Anthropic will' adhere.

claims.claim: On CBS (February 28, 2026): 'we need to have a conversation about accountability, about who is holding the button and who can say no'; 'Disagreeing with the government is the most American thing in the world. And we are patriots.' (The repair cut his 'We don't want to sell something that we don't think is reliable' line, which repeated the statement's reliability argument.)
claims.passage: Amodei framed the fight as a question of oversight, "about who is holding the button and who can say no," and of loyalty: "Disagreeing with the government is the most American thing in the world. And we are patriots."
claims.inference: Defiance of authority paired with professed loyalty to the country.
claims.alternative: Broadcast messaging in a legal and commercial fight.

claims.claim: He told CBS: 'It's about the principle of standing up for what's right.'
claims.passage: He called the Pentagon fight "the principle of standing up for what's right," the Type 1 reading's best line
claims.inference: Principle language; the strongest Type 1 datum in the dispute. The article keeps it next to the motive-level 6-versus-1 separation (C125).
claims.alternative: Standard advocacy rhetoric.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the February 2026 dispute combined defiance of the most powerful authority available with professions of loyalty ('we are patriots', C84; 'much more in common with the Department of War', C177). This is consistent with a Six, but equally with a One's principled stand and with ordinary litigation strategy: the patriot and common-ground lines came with a $200 million military contract (Fortune, S18; CNBC, S20) and all federal business (AP, S19) at stake. The counterphobic-subtype label is removed (critic-04, enneagram-06).
claims.passage: Defying the most powerful authority available while professing loyalty fits a Six, but it fits a One's principled stand and ordinary litigation strategy too: the patriot and common-ground lines came with a $200 million military contract and all federal business at stake.
claims.inference: Consistent with Six, not proof; the episode cannot count against or for Six on its own.
claims.alternative: One (principled stand) or incentive (litigation and contract) readings fit the same behavior.

type_hypothesis.against: Real evidence resists Type 6. (1) The Five markers are well sourced: in 2023 he said he had 'deliberately tried to be a little bit low profile because I want to defend my ability to think about things intellectually in a way that's different from other people and isn't tinged by the approval of other people' (C184); he writes partly to clarify his own thinking (C185, paraphrased); one direct report, which TechCrunch quotes him calling 'incredibly freeing', with time protected for big-picture work (C187, C38); long-document thinking (C36); frugality and embarrassment at his new station (C175); his first thought on giving up on OpenAI was another lab, and he was initially skeptical of the group exit (C174, C115); his stated stance under pressure leans on study, proportion and calm (C208). By the page's own test these are Five facts (C196). (2) Institution-building (RSP and trust, evaluators, joint governance, the pacing statement) does not discriminate 5 from 6 (C146). (3) Much of the threat-modeling and regulation advocacy is his profession, his company's strategy and his milieu (C60, C90, C131, C132, C133, C153), and rules he proposes also bind rivals (C161); much of the 2026 trust talk is CEO messaging in a documentary, federal-fight and IPO year (C133). Trust is also AI safety's working vocabulary (C206). (4) The OpenAI exit sequence fits a leverage/turf reading as well as a trust reading (C115, C114), and the Lex exit answer is mostly about vision and influence by example (C25, C118). (5) Type 1 has real support: Kantrowitz's 'strident sense of the way things should be' (C221), parental right-and-wrong (C04), 'cannot in good conscience' and 'standing up for what's right' (C50, C85), abrasiveness (C112); his anger targets misrepresentation, which does not discriminate 1 from 6 (C222). (6) Recognition and exclusion (C23, C73, C121, C228) fit neither 5 nor 6. (7) Steady confidence in his own forecasts (C41) is a real cost to the Six reading. (8) The 2026 Bloomberg pressure and exit statements (C179, C181, C185, C208) rest on local machine transcripts awaiting a human re-listen and are paraphrased, not quoted.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 5 (the previously published reading, C239) remains the strongest rival. Its motive is security through mastery and self-sufficiency, and it explains: the 2023 wish to protect his independent thinking from 'the approval of other people' (C184); writing to clarify his thinking (C185); long-document leadership (C36); protecting his time with one direct report (C38, C187); frugality and embarrassment at status (C175); DeepMind as his first thought and skepticism of a group exit (C174); calm, proportion and study under pressure (C208); and the Lex exit answer's emphasis on vision and a 'clean experiment' (C25, C118). A Five who has learned to rely on a tested few would look much like the record (C65). Type 1 is close behind: Kantrowitz's 'strident sense of the way things should be' (C221), duty language (C04), principled red lines (C50, C85) and abrasiveness (C112); it is weakened, modestly, by his habit of arguing lines through reliability and who holds the button rather than his own rightness (C125, C89), by Marre's 'I never saw someone engaged in a strong moral or ethical quest' (C15) and by the Gulf-money pragmatism (C31). Type 3 (recognition) fails on the 2023 low profile and the embarrassment at status (C229). Type 8 is weakened by his shutting down the 2023 offer to run a merged OpenAI-Anthropic (C32), though the control strand (C30, C78, C134, C227) keeps it from being dismissed.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What he leans on when the ground moves (C63): a Five on its own understanding and a guarded store of time and energy; a Six on people and promises it has tested. Worry, intellect and institution-building do not separate them (C146), and neither does his 2026 vocabulary: he called both one direct report and his talks to the whole company 'freeing', but both spare him one-on-one demands, so the pair illustrates rather than decides (C188). The discriminating evidence is costly choices, most of them before 2026: (a) at OpenAI, what he tracked was being misled (Roose: 'biggest concern was about Altman's character', a record of times he felt misled, C198, C235, C174), and in his own account Altman would agree and nothing would change (C21; OpenAI's stance that safety has been a constant, C189); he left with six colleagues and later said he should have left sooner (C26, C171, C117); in 2026 he named distrust, not disagreement, as the reason to leave (C181, paraphrased) (C236). The leverage/turf reading fits the same steps and the group exit was Kaplan's idea (C115), so this leans Six without settling it. (b) Whom he built around: equal equity for seven co-founders against near-universal advice (C79), trust as his organizing word from 2022, before Anthropic had a product (C172, C237), Daniela's on-record account of a 40-year bond and a founding team the siblings had managed (C173, C166), and an executive team routed through his sister so that the time he guards is guarded by her (C187, C188). (c) Under pressure, his accounts cut both ways: study, proportion and calm (C208) versus turning to the whole company so that he never feels alone (C179) (C209). Against Type 1, his lines arrive through reliability and who holds the button rather than his own rightness (C125, C89); anger does not discriminate (C222). Against Type 8, he shut down the 2023 offer to run a merged OpenAI-Anthropic (C32). Milieu and commercial stakes can explain much of the 2026 trust talk, so the Six reading leans on the pre-commercial record (C133). Limitation: the 2026 Bloomberg statements (C179, C181, C185, C208) come from local machine transcripts awaiting a human re-listen and are paraphrased.

(5) How much of the safety-institution building is personality rather than strategy or milieu (C60, C90, C131, C132, C133, C153, C161).
